A project starts with a mapping file that lists your samples, and one command
that sets up the project folder. After that, everything happens in the app, the
same way as in [Get started](RiboPilot.html).

# The mapping file

The mapping file is a CSV file with one row per sample. For example:

```
ID,Taxon,R1,R2,Voucher
Fish_01,Brosme brosme,Fish_01_R1.fastq.gz,Fish_01_R2.fastq.gz,USNM 123456
Fish_02,Upeneus parvus,SRR22396758/SRR22396758_1.fastq.gz,SRR22396758/SRR22396758_2.fastq.gz,USNM 123457
Snail_01,Tritia reticulata,Snail_01_R1.fq.gz,Snail_01_R2.fq.gz,
```

The rules:

- **Columns.** It needs the columns `ID`, `Taxon`, `R1`, and `R2`. Upper and
  lower case do not matter in column names.
- **IDs.** Each ID must be unique, ignoring case, and at most 18 characters
  long. Use only letters, digits, dash (`-`), underscore (`_`), and colon
  (`:`): no spaces, dots, or slashes. IDs are kept exactly as you typed them,
  leading zeros included.
- **Commas only.** Save the file with commas between values. From Excel, use
  File > Save As > CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited).
- **Paired reads only.** Every sample with reads needs both an `R1` and an `R2`
  file. Single-end reads are not supported.
- **Read file names** are relative to the read folder you pass as `data_path`.
  Subfolders are fine (`SRR22396758/SRR22396758_1.fastq.gz`), but full paths
  are not.
- **No spaces or special characters in paths.** File names, folder names, and
  the project path may use only letters, digits, and `.`, `_`, `-`, and `/`.
  RiboPilot stops and names each path it cannot pass to Docker, Singularity, or
  Nextflow, for example one with a space or a quote mark.
- **Extra columns** are kept, and you can use them in your GenBank headers, for
  example as `{Voucher}`. A column name with a space or a dash is read with a
  dot in its place, so `Voucher ID` becomes `{Voucher.ID}`. The **Available
  columns** list in the Export window shows every name.
- **Reserved names.** RiboPilot adds some columns itself, so your file cannot
  use these names: taxid, sci_name, rank, match_type, tax_alternatives,
  lineage, lineage_taxids, ref_id, user_group, ref_source, taxonomy_switch,
  taxonomy_lock, and time_stamp.

The IDs end up in your GenBank records, so choose them with care.

# Create the project

```r
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads"
)
```

RiboPilot checks the mapping file and the read files before it writes
anything, and stops with a message that names each problem. The analysis runs in
Docker by default. On a computing cluster, pass your cluster profile as
`executor`; see [Running on a cluster](Clusters.html).

An NCBI API key is optional; see [Installation](Installation.html) for where to
put it.

Then open the app and follow the five steps, as in
[Get started](RiboPilot.html):

```r
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("~/my_project")
```

Do the Reference step before you assemble.

# Already have an assembly?

If you have a genome assembly for a sample, or just the contig that holds its
ribosomal repeat, you can use it instead of assembling from reads. Add an
`Assembly` column to your mapping file naming that sample's FASTA file, and pass
the folder that holds them as `assembly_path`:

```r
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path          = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn    = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path     = "~/my_reads",
  assembly_path = "~/my_assemblies"
)
```

RiboPilot searches each supplied assembly for rRNA genes and carries forward the
contigs that carry an 18S or 28S anchor; the rest are recorded and left behind.
A single ribosomal contig passes this search without doing anything special. If
you supplied a fragment too short to carry an anchor (an ITS-only sequence, for
example), turn the search off in the app's **Assembly Options** and RiboPilot
uses your file exactly as given.

A sample with an assembly does not need reads: leave its `R1` and `R2` blank.
If your file has no reads at all, you can leave out the `R1` and `R2` columns
and `data_path`. The assembly files must be FASTA, all gzipped (`.gz`) or all
plain in one project, and named relative to `assembly_path`.

A sample with no reads gets no depth profile, since there is nothing to map
back; every other step runs the same. If you do have its reads, name them
anyway, and RiboPilot uses them for depth while still starting from your
assembly.

# Adding samples later

To add samples to a project you have already started, write a mapping file that
lists only the new samples, and run:

```r
RiboPilot::add_samples(
  "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/more_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads"
)
```

It runs the same checks as `new_project()`, and refuses IDs that are already in
the project. Put the new read files in the same folder as the project's other
reads (the `data_path` you gave `new_project()`): runs look for reads there.
The new samples then appear in the Taxonomy step, ready to assign.

To fix or add metadata, such as a voucher number, for samples that are already
in the project, list them in a mapping file with the new values and run
`RiboPilot::update_sample_metadata()` the same way. It never changes a sample's
reads, assembly, state, or locks.

Do not rerun `new_project()` with `force = TRUE` on a project you have worked
on: it deletes all its results.

# What is in the project folder

The project folder holds your results database, its settings, and the
pipeline's working files. The table in
[Disk space, caches, and offline use](Caches-and-Offline.html) says what each
item is, and which you can delete.
